The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI), digital learning environments, and data-driven educational technologies is transforming the professional responsibilities of teachers and creating new demands for ethical and pedagogical decision-making. This paper examines the theoretical foundations of developing teachers’ professional-deontological competence in the context of digital transformation. The study aims to conceptualize professional-deontological competence as an integrated capacity encompassing ethical knowledge, professional responsibility, pedagogical judgment, digital ethics, and reflective practice. A conceptual and analytical approach is employed to examine relevant philosophical perspectives, contemporary teacher competency frameworks, and emerging challenges associated with AI-supported education. The analysis identifies five interrelated dimensions of professional-deontological competence: ethical and normative awareness, value-based professional commitment, responsible pedagogical decision-making, digital and AI ethics, and reflective professional development. The paper argues that effective teacher education should move beyond the transmission of professional codes toward the systematic integration of ethical reasoning into authentic pedagogical situations. It proposes a conceptual framework combining case-based learning, ethical dilemma analysis, reflective practice, and responsible AI use. The paper concludes that strengthening professional-deontological competence is essential for preserving teacher agency, protecting learners’ dignity, and ensuring that technological innovation remains consistent with the humanistic purposes of education. The proposed framework requires further empirical investigation to establish its effectiveness across different educational contexts.

Abstract Background Generative AI is now routine in student work, yet instruments measuring the risks attached to that use—over-reliance, misuse, and the reflective practices that guard against them—remain scarce in African higher education. This study reports the initial development and exploratory evaluation of a 23-item Student Susceptibility to AI (SAI) item pool. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 408 students, recruited by convenience sampling at six purposively selected Ghanaian institutions, was analysed using a reverse-coding audit, Principal Axis Factoring with Promax rotation, parallel analysis, false-discovery-rate-corrected comparisons and multivariable regression. No pilot preceded the survey, and one sample informed item evaluation and extraction. Results Two-thirds of participants (65.7%) reported daily AI use; only 2.0% none. Parallel analysis supported three factors, the fourth eigenvalue falling below the random threshold; both solutions are reported. Internal consistency was acceptable for Over-Reliance, Cognitive Vulnerability and Resilience & Reflection (α = 0.807–0.824) but inadequate for Misuse/Academic Integrity (α = 0.535), and a total composite was unsupported (ECV = 0.373). Use frequency produced the largest group differences of any variable examined, though adjusted predictors explained only 2.7–7.9% of variance. Conclusion AI use is already near-universal here, so the question is not whether students use these tools but how. Reflective verification practices proved largely independent of the risk dimensions, indicating that susceptibility is not simply a function of use intensity: interventions should target how students interrogate AI output, not how often they consult it. The item pool remains promising but unstable, requiring revision and independent confirmation.

documents.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs) remain a major occupational health challenge, and automotive service work is a high-risk context involving awkward postures, repetitive tasks, and sustained static loading. Conventional ergonomic tools capture static posture snapshots and do not reflect how musculoskeletal stress accumulates over time. This study developed the Manual Integrated Ergonomics Risk Assessment Tool (MIERAT), a low-cost, observation-based framework for resource-constrained automotive settings, and conducted an initial field validation. MIERAT combines REBA-based posture severity (PS), exposure duration (D), and a calibrated Time Modifier (TM; 1.0–2.5) into a Cumulative Risk Index (CRI = PS × D × TM), grounded in biomechanical loading theory and aligned with ISO 11226, ISO 11228-1, and ISO 45001. Expert panel review yielded an S-CVI/Ave of 0.95, indicating strong content validity. Duration–CRI associations were very strong for under-vehicle servicing (ρ = 0.910), tyre fitment (ρ = 0.961), and brake/suspension repair (ρ = 0.945), all p < 0.001. Because duration enters the CRI equation directly and also determines the TM, these correlations are mathematically expected; they show that the index behaves as designed but are not independent evidence of construct validity. Inter-rater reliability across three observers was excellent (ICC = 0.975–0.997), with moderate-to-perfect categorical agreement (weighted κ = 0.557–1.000). Task-level profiling identified tyre demounting, wheel alignment, and drain plug loosening as dominant ergonomic hotspots. These findings provide preliminary support for MIERAT as a content-valid and reliable tool for profiling cumulative postural exposure and planning ergonomic interventions in South African automotive workshops. Validation against independent outcomes, such as musculoskeletal symptoms, fatigue, biomechanical loading, or injury data, is needed to establish its construct and predictive validity.

documents.abstract: This study aimed to develop automotive occupational health and safety learning multimedia and examine changes in students’ learning interest after its use. The study employed a research and development approach using the ADDIE model and a one-group pretest–posttest design involving 31 Grade 10 automotive engineering students. Data were collected using a 20-item learning interest questionnaire. Expert validation results indicated that the multimedia was highly feasible, with scores exceeding 87%. All questionnaire items were valid, with Cronbach’s alpha values of 0.890 for the pretest and 0.843 for the posttest. The mean learning interest score increased from 70.03 to 86.61, with a normalized gain of 55.52%, categorized as moderate. A one-sample t-test showed that the posttest mean was significantly higher than the reference value of 70 (p < 0.001). These findings suggest that the multimedia has potential to support students’ learning interest. However, the absence of a control group limits causal conclusions.

This article theoretically analyzes the didactic possibilities of artificial intelligence technologies in pedagogical education and the directions for their use in improving the professional training of future teachers. It highlights opportunities for individualizing learning, creating and adapting educational materials, tracking progress, providing prompt feedback, and supporting independent learning. Issues regarding the application of generative artificial intelligence and adaptive learning systems in tasks aimed at developing pedagogical design, critical thinking, and professional reflection are considered.

documents.abstract: Modern administrative governance is undergoing a systemic socio-technical reconfiguration, transitioning rapidly from manual, paper-bound ledgers and legacy e-governance architectures to integrated digital public infrastructure and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) co-pilot environments. This evolution demands an expanded conceptualization of workforce digital readiness. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), this study systematically examines the operational demands, capacity deficits, and governance challenges confronting administrative personnel across public sector and higher education institutions, particularly within resource-constrained regional environments. Evaluating an integrated dual-layer competency framework—encompassing core computing proficiencies (advanced spreadsheet manipulation, relational database taxonomy, cloud-based records management, and virtual collaboration) alongside emerging Generative AI capabilities (contextual prompt engineering, automated text summarization, cross-linguistic translation, and critical output verification across platforms such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Copilot)—this paper articulates the comparative operational advantages and structural friction points defining modern public administration. Systemic capacity gaps are identified, including technological anxiety, shallow digital literacy, cybersecurity hygiene vulnerabilities, acute geographical infrastructure disparities (exemplified by power grid instability and bandwidth limitations in regional campus settings), and administrative risks surrounding AI hallucinations and data privacy. To bridge the divide between top-down digital governance policies and ground-level workplace execution, we articulate a multi-tiered strategic roadmap incorporating task-oriented contextual training, robust institutional AI governance frameworks, peer-mentorship coaching networks, and sustained capital infrastructure investments, paired with individual lifelong learning pathways. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that while automated tools and AI engines serve as powerful efficiency enablers, rigorous human oversight, procedural discretion, and ethical boundary-setting remain mandatory to safeguard due process, institutional accountability, and transparent governance.

Background: Emergency departments are cognitively demanding environments where healthcare professionals are frequently exposed to interruptions and other distracting factors that may compromise workflow and patient safety. This systematic review aimed to identify factors that distract healthcare professionals in emergency departments and to synthesise their cognitive, organisational, and patient-safety consequences from a cognitive ergonomics perspective. Methods: A systematic literature review was conducted in PubMed, CINAHL Ultimate, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement. Studies meeting predefined eligibility criteria were included. Methodological quality was assessed using design-specific critical appraisal tools, and findings were synthesised using inductive content analysis. Results: Nineteen studies met the predefined eligibility criteria and were included in the synthesis. The most frequently reported distraction-related phenomena included communication-related interruptions, telephone calls, and technological and environmental disturbances, while multitasking and task switching were identified as related work processes or responses to competing demands. Across the studies, distraction-related phenomena were associated with cognitive and workflow consequences, including increased workload, reduced situation awareness, work-related stress, and workflow disruption. Only one of the 19 included studies directly examined task errors, whereas the others identified interruptions during medication-related activities and potential safety concerns without directly measuring medication errors or patient harm. Several studies also identified clinically relevant interruptions associated with information exchange and care coordination, alongside unnecessary or poorly timed interruptions that were perceived as disruptive. Conclusions: Distraction-related phenomena are common features of emergency department work and are associated with cognitive and workflow outcomes. However, direct evidence regarding clinical errors and patient safety outcomes remains limited, and the available findings do not establish a causal relationship between distraction-related phenomena and patient harm. Potential cognitive-ergonomic strategies may focus on reducing avoidable and low-value interruptions while preserving clinically necessary communication that supports information exchange and care coordination; however, their effectiveness requires empirical evaluation.

documents.abstract: AI-for-Science agents are increasingly being used for formulating scientific hypotheses, running autonomous experiments, and interpreting evidence. These agents are constructed by integrating a large language model (LLM) into a domain-specific agent harness, which in turn can improve the LLM's scientific capability and enable the model to orchestrate scientific tools. In this work, we ask whether model safety is preserved when an LLM is integrated in an AI-for-Science agent harness. We evaluate five agent harnesses on 50 harmful chemistry requests. Specifically, we study how the safety behavior changes under direct prompting, two simple adversarial prompting strategies, and an adaptive attack. Across four recent GPT variants, our results show that the agent harness can increase harmful compliance even under direct prompting. More critically, we find that adaptive attacks that are largely unsuccessful against the base LLM suddenly become highly successful after the agent harness is introduced. Our results show that the safety behavior of the base LLM is not durable once a harness is introduced. Thus, as AI-for-Science agents become more capable and autonomous, the community needs to evaluate and align the agent using domain-specific safety benchmarks.

documents.abstract: Abstract Creativity is a fundamental part of cultural evolution, but the mechanisms by which groups produce novelty are notoriously difficult to infer from the historical record. Iterated learning experiments have shown that cultural transmission reliably distorts artifacts toward the inductive biases of learners, but most of this work uses linear chains of human participants, and it is unclear how these dynamics play out in the networked, human-AI systems that increasingly shape cultural production. In this study, we analyze one such system: Artbreeder, which hosts daily “remix parties” in which users iteratively build on each other's work from a single seed image, producing branching lineages of images co-created by humans and generative AI. Using 130,882 images from 368 remix parties over 13 months, we find that images become less novel over the course of a party and that each remix step moves less far from its parents, consistent with the stabilization seen in iterated learning experiments, and that late-stage images drift toward the platform's dominant portrait style. More novel “parent” images produce more novel and more complex “children.” More novel children attract more likes but are not remixed more, whereas more complex children are remixed less. Finally, larger remix parties produce images that are more novel but less complex.

The study aimed to examine the effect of trust in AI on Human-AI relationship among university students. A cross-sectional survey research design was used. The sample comprised 300 university students (150 males and 150 females) selected through convenient sampling technique. Measures included the General Attitude toward AI Scale (GAAIS) by Schepman and Rodway (32 items, Positive α = .84, Negative α = .73), Short Trust in Automation Scale (S-TIAS) by McGrath et al. (3 items, α = .88), and Experiences in Human-AI Relationships Scale (EHARS) by Yang and Oshio (7 items). Correlation analysis showed that trust in AI was positively correlated with Human-AI relationship. The study contributed to the growing literature on Human-AI relationships by highlighting the role of trust in AI in Human-AI interactions among university students. The findings have important implications for AI literacy, technology acceptance, and the development of educational interventions aimed at fostering healthy and effective Human-AI relationships.

This study determined the effect of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted pedagogy on the problem-solving skills of first-year Bachelor of Secondary Education students enrolled in Mathematics in the Modern World at Urdaneta City University. The study was completed in May 2026 during School Year 2025-2026. Using a quasi-experimental pre-test and post-test non-equivalent group design, the researchers compared the performance of students taught through conventional pedagogy with those who experienced AI-supported instruction. Problem-solving performance was examined using George Pólya's four-step framework: understanding the problem, planning a solution, carrying out the plan, and checking the solution. Initial results showed that both groups had limited problem-solving skills before instruction, especially in planning, execution, and verification. After the intervention, both groups improved; however, students exposed to AI-assisted pedagogy obtained stronger gains, particularly in carrying out the plan and overall problem-solving performance. The paired-samples t-test indicated significant improvement within the experimental group, while the independent-samples t-test showed that the experimental group outperformed the conventional group in selected post-test measures. The findings suggest that AI tools, when used with teacher guidance and structured problem-solving activities, can support mathematical learning by offering immediate feedback, alternative explanations, and opportunities for solution checking. The study further indicates that AI should be integrated as a cognitive support rather than as a substitute for independent reasoning.

documents.abstract: Robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) has transformed minimally invasive procedures by improving physical ergonomics, surgical field visualisation and instrument manipulation. However, RAS introduces unique cognitive load for the surgeon. Cognitive ergonomics aims to enhance the mental resources to optimise the interactions between surgeons and their environment, thereby improving the wellbeing and performance of surgeons and patient outcomes. Current evidence highlights that RAS redistributes, rather than eliminates, ergonomic burden from the physical to the mental domain. Subjective measurement tools remain the most widely used; however, physiological measures offer continuous and real-time data regarding cognitive workload fluctuations during surgery. Strategies to improve cognitive ergonomics include surgeon-level strategies, interface and system design alterations, operating room workflow optimisation, incorporation of artificial intelligence, and training and education. This narrative review summarises the current evidence regarding the mental demands associated with RAS, cognitive workload measures, the consequences of poor cognition, and emerging strategies to improve cognitive ergonomics in RAS.

This study analyzes how citizens identify gender biases in narratives generated by artificial intelligence (AI), using ChatGPT as a case study. An online experiment was conducted with 614 Spanish participants, randomly assigned to three conditions: a professional success narrative featuring a female protagonist, a narrative featuring a male protagonist, and a neutral narrative. After exposure, gender bias detection in the story, perceived bias in ChatGPT, and the intention to reduce or correct algorithmic biases were measured. The results show that the narrative featuring a female protagonist was associated with higher bias detection and greater attribution of partiality to ChatGPT. No significant differences were observed according to participants’ gender or educational level. Likewise, indicators of proximity to AI, such as interest in these technologies and the use of AI-based applications, were associated with lower perceived bias in the tool. The findings underscore the need to promote critical AI literacy that helps citizens more critically recognize when its outputs reproduce gender stereotypes or inequalities.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may assist evidence-informed health-policy work, but favorable user perceptions and well-written outputs do not establish factual reliability or implementation readiness. A multilevel mixed-methods pilot evaluation examined MUSYA AI, a locally grounded policy-support platform in Thailand. Thirty-five health-sector personnel completed questionnaires, seven participated in Think-Aloud observation, sixteen Policy Briefs were assessed using an expert rubric, and seventy factual claims underwent evidence auditing. The document comparison included eight MUSYA AI and eight ChatGPT (GPT-5.6, OpenAI) outputs under common task instructions and system-specific information access. Mean System Usability Scale, perceived usefulness, and trust scores were 97.29/100, 4.70/5, and 4.57/5, respectively. Ceiling effects and limited internal consistency constrained interpretation of these descriptive indices; user experience, ease of use, and behavioral intention were interpreted at the item level. Observations documented reading and editing, but successful error detection and correction were not evaluated. MUSYA AI documents received higher overall quality ratings than comparator documents (95.38 ± 2.39 versus 72.25 ± 11.90; difference, 23.13 points; bootstrap 95% confidence interval, 15.63–31.38; Hedges’ g = 2.55). However, classification–rationale inconsistencies affected forty-five claims (64.3%), leaving comparative factual-accuracy findings provisional. The small, nonrandomized document sample and absence of verified task pairing prevented causal attribution of quality differences. MUSYA AI elicited favorable pilot-user perceptions and produced higher-rated documents within the evaluated sample. These findings support continued supervised evaluation; institutional readiness requires traceable claim adjudication, demonstrated oversight effectiveness, and broader controlled assessment.

documents.abstract: Children with dyslexia often experience persistent challenges in reading, motivation, and self-regulation within traditional classroom settings that rely on uniform instructional approaches. With the growing integration of artificial intelligence in education, AI-based adaptive learning systems have emerged as innovative tools capable of personalizing instruction and supporting diverse learning needs. This study investigated the effect of AI-based adaptive learning systems on reading performance, motivation, and self-regulation among primary school students with dyslexia in Abuja, Nigeria. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control group design was adopted, with a sample of 60 Primary 5 pupils drawn from selected inclusive and special education schools in the Abuja Municipal Area. Data were collected using a Reading Performance Test, Motivation toward Reading Scale, and Self-Regulation in Reading Questionnaire, and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including independent samples t-test. Findings revealed that students exposed to AI-based adaptive learning demonstrated significantly higher improvements across all variables compared to those receiving conventional instruction. The experimental group recorded substantial gains in reading performance (mean gain = 24.20), motivation (mean gain = 1.50), and self-regulation (mean gain = 1.60), compared to the control group. Statistical analysis confirmed that these differences were significant (p < 0.05). These findings align with Cognitive Load Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development. The study concludes that AI-based adaptive learning systems offer an effective approach for improving both academic and psychological outcomes among students with dyslexia. It recommends the integration of AI-driven instructional tools in primary education, alongside teacher training and policy support, to promote inclusive, personalized, and effective learning environments.

documents.abstract: Automated government case management is moving from digitised workflow toward intelligent triage, eligibility assessment, risk prioritisation and service routing. In Saudi Arabia, this transition is especially consequential because digital government programmes increasingly connect high-volume public services with data-intensive decision processes. The central challenge is not simply whether artificial intelligence can accelerate case handling, but whether decisions can remain timely, reviewable, understandable and contestable when models operate at operational speed. This review examines how explainable artificial intelligence and real-time decisioning can be combined for automated government case management in Saudi Arabia. It synthesises thirty DOI-verified studies published from 2020 to 2025 across explainability, human-AI decision support, public-sector algorithmic governance, Saudi digital government and streaming analytics. The review develops a socio-technical framework in which case intake, data quality, machine reasoning, rule validation, explanation generation, human oversight, notification, appeal and continuous monitoring form one auditable decision loop. The analysis finds that explainability is valuable only when it is matched to the decision recipient and linked to operational controls; generic feature-attribution displays alone do not guarantee justified or trustworthy outcomes. Real-time systems also require explicit latency budgets, uncertainty handling, concept-drift monitoring and escalation rules so that speed does not suppress due process. For Saudi public agencies, successful adoption depends on combining interoperable data, secure governance, accountable ownership and Arabic-capable explanation interfaces with measurable human override and appeal mechanisms. The study proposes evaluation criteria spanning predictive validity, explanation fidelity, decision latency, fairness, reviewability and institutional accountability. It concludes that explainable real-time case management should be designed as governed decision infrastructure rather than as an isolated prediction model.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is increasingly important for ensuring transparency and trust in neural systems; however, its applicability to creative text generation remains limited. Neural poetry generation models produce linguistically coherent and stylistically rich outputs, yet explaining decisions such as metaphor construction, emotional tone, and thematic development remains unresolved. This systematic literature review synthesizes 26 peer‐reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2026, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a predefined protocol across four major digital libraries. The analysis identifies a fundamental mismatch between existing XAI paradigms and the properties of generative modeling. We propose a taxonomy distinguishing classification‐native methods from generation‐compatible approaches, highlighting their differing assumptions. Based on established criteria of contrastivity, selectivity, and faithfulness, we show that attention mechanisms lack causal validity as explanatory tools. To consolidate these findings, we introduce a unified failure framework comprising five interacting structural limitations: token–semantic mismatch, attention non‐causality, classification–generation incompatibility, evaluation collapse, and human–model ontological misalignment. These limitations collectively constrain the effectiveness of current XAI methods in creative contexts. Our findings indicate that advancing explainability in neural poetry generation requires a shift toward semantic‐level representations, causal intervention‐based approaches, and human‐centered evaluation frameworks that incorporate aesthetic and interpretive dimensions.

Automated decision-making systems increasingly influence healthcare, finance, recruitment, education, public administration, and digital platforms. Although advanced machine-learning models can discover complex relationships, their opaque reasoning can obstruct auditing, contestability, and safe deployment. This narrative review examines how explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) may improve transparency and reliability by clarifying model behavior, revealing data dependencies, supporting error detection, and enabling informed human oversight. It synthesizes established work on interpretable modeling, local feature attribution, surrogate explanations, counterfactual reasoning, explanation evaluation, and governance. A conceptual assurance framework connects data provenance, predictive validation, explanation fidelity, subgroup analysis, and operational monitoring. The paper distinguishes understandable explanations from evidence that a system is accurate, robust, or fair: an attractive explanation alone does not establish reliability. A non-empirical diagram illustrates complementary assurance dimensions without implying measured results. Practical implications include tailoring explanations to decision recipients, testing explanation stability under perturbations, documenting uncertainty, and establishing appeal mechanisms. The review concludes that XAI is most effective when embedded within a wider socio-technical accountability process rather than deployed as a stand-alone visualization technique.

Abstract Background Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults’ digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships. Objective This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults’ instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55‐86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI. Results DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=−0.455, 95% BCa CI −0.632 to −0.229; P <.001) but did not significantly affect fear of personal failure ( P =.12) or human-machine ambiguity ( P =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=−0.215, 95% BCa CI −0.410 to −0.009; P =.05 and β=−0.211, 95% BCa CI −0.389 to −0.001; P =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203; P =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075; P =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518; P =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI −0.002 to 0.116). Conclusions DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults’ specific technological fears and practical barriers.

Digital transformation is opening new avenues for innovating fire fighting and rescue training, drills, and command operations, steering them toward visualization, data-driven methodologies, and measurability. This article analyzes the scientific foundations and practical applications of fire simulation, digital scenarios, virtual reality, augmented reality, and digital twins in enhancing situational awareness, tactical decision-making, and inter-agency coordination capabilities. Building on this framework, the paper proposes key solutions, including establishing a digital scenario bank, standardizing scenario structures, integrating digital simulations with field-based training, developing command simulation training centers, and building digital capabilities for instructors, officers, and firefighters.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the content of accounting work, but the career consequences of that change remain less clear in emerging economies. Using field responses from 600 accounting and finance professionals in Nigeria, Ghana, and Kenya (200 per country), this paper examines whether intensive AI use is associated with professional role transformation, whether role transformation is associated with competence evolution, and whether those evolving competencies are linked to career sustainability. Learning and organizational support is considered both as a contextual resource and as a potential moderator. The analysis uses multi-item composite measures, HC3-robust path regressions, 5,000-resample bootstrapping, effect-size estimates, 10-fold cross-validation, and exploratory country comparisons. AI adoption was positively associated with role transformation (β = .491, p < .001). AI adoption (β = .286, p < .001) and role transformation (β = .462, p < .001) jointly explained 42.6% of the variance in competence evolution, while competence evolution was positively associated with career sustainability (β = .414, p < .001). The direct role-transformation effect on career sustainability was negligible (β = .013, p = .764), whereas the indirect effect through competence evolution was significant (β = .192, 95% bootstrap CI [.146, .242]). The serial pathway from AI adoption through role transformation and competence evolution to career sustainability was also significant (β = .094, 95% CI [.069, .123]). Learning and organizational support had a positive main effect but did not moderate the competence-sustainability relationship. The results suggest that the long-term value of AI-related role change depends less on the fact that work changes than on whether professionals acquire the digital, analytical, advisory, and ethical capabilities needed to succeed in the redesigned role. Keywords: artificial intelligence; accounting profession; role transformation; competence evolution; career sustainability; emerging economies; Africa; human capital.

documents.abstract: (1) Background: Generative and, increasingly, agentic artificial intelligence (AI) are reshaping how firms create, deliver, and capture value. Yet business model innovation (BMI) research often assumes that humans retain design authority while digital technologies support analysis or execute predefined decisions. This assumption becomes contestable when AI systems can generate value-bearing artifacts, participate in organizational decision-making, and undertake goal-directed action within delegated boundaries. (2) Approach: Integrating business-model and activity-system research, dynamic capabilities, socio-technical and human–AI decision-making perspectives, and research on generative and agentic AI, this concept paper develops a framework that distinguishes three logics of AI-enabled BMI: a supporting logic (AI as instrument), a generative logic (AI as co-creator), and an agentic logic (AI as delegated economic actor). The framework distinguishes business-model operation from business-model innovation and identifies delegated reconfiguration authority as a key condition under which agentic action can constitute BMI. (3) Contribution: The paper advances six propositions explaining how AI redistributes ideation, decision, execution, and reconfiguration rights; how machine agency may compress the interval between business-model reconfigurations; how value-capture mechanisms may change; and why complementary capabilities, governance, and legitimacy remain decisive. (4) Conclusions: The paper offers a focused research agenda centered on agency allocation and decision rights, the temporal dynamics and measurement of BMI, and value capture and governance in agent-mediated business models. It thereby provides a more precise theoretical basis for distinguishing autonomous operation within a business model from autonomous or semi-autonomous reconfiguration of the business model itself.

The growing integration of artificial intelligence into governance challenges the conditions under which political authority can be considered legitimate. Algorithmic systems increasingly mediate decisions that shape citizens’ lives, yet their operations frequently bypass human judgment and obscure the justificatory basis of political authority. This article reinterprets John Locke’s political philosophy as a normative framework for assessing algorithmic authority. By reconstructing Locke’s account of reason, equality, consent, and fiduciary trust, it brings his political anthropology into dialogue with contemporary debates on algorithmic accountability and digital constitutionalism. The article argues that AI governance does not merely raise technical or regulatory problems; it threatens the conditions under which citizens can understand, evaluate, and contest the exercise of power. Because many AI systems operate through models that neither officials nor citizens can meaningfully interpret, they generate forms of automated prerogative that weaken the fiduciary relationship between governors and governed. Against this danger, the article advances a Lockean criterion for computational governance: algorithmic authority can be considered legitimate only insofar as it preserves intelligibility, fiduciary accountability, and contestability. Legitimacy cannot be restored through technical adjustment alone; it requires institutional conditions under which power remains publicly intelligible, politically answerable, and open to challenge by those subject to it.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizational decision-making, managerial roles, and accountability, yet responsible AI governance remains dominated by principles, technical controls, and regulatory compliance. This conceptual paper develops a human leadership-based framework for translating responsible AI principles into organizational governance. In the framework, the responsible leader is an accountable human organizational actor—such as a board member, senior executive, business leader, or designated decision owner—while AI is treated as a governed technological system or operational agent rather than the accountable leader. Human responsible leadership influences responsible AI governance (RAIG) capability through six mediating organizational processes: stakeholder orientation, ethical sensemaking, accountability architecture, meaningful human oversight, inclusive participation, and long-term value orientation. RAIG capability is defined as the higher-order organizational capacity to institutionalize and adapt lifecycle governance arrangements; it enables observable governance practices, which are conceptually separated from downstream responsible AI outcomes. AI operational autonomy is proposed as a focal moderator: the leadership-to-RAIG pathway should become stronger when AI can initiate or execute consequential actions with limited contemporaneous human approval, particularly where actions are difficult to reverse, trace, or interrupt. The framework offers testable propositions and a research agenda, but it is conceptual and requires empirical validation; it is not a technical safety guarantee.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in digital multimodal composing (DMC) presents both opportunities and challenges for second language (L2) research and pedagogy. While GenAI tools provide linguistic and multimodal support, they also raise concerns about biased information, culturally generic outputs, and technological overreliance. This qualitative study investigates L2 students' enactment of critical digital literacies (CDL) during GenAI‐assisted video composing. Drawing on CDL as a theoretical orientation and the analytical heuristic of critical awareness, critical identities, critical relationships, and critical actions, the study examines how students negotiated and revised AI‐generated video representations. Using multimodal critical discourse analysis of screen recordings, final video artifacts, focus group interviews, and reflective essays from 20 L2 students, the findings reveal four interrelated forms of CDL enactment. Students demonstrated critical awareness of GenAI's culturally limited outputs, authored critical identities through multimodal redesign, negotiated critical relationships with peers and GenAI, and engaged in localized critical action against cultural erasure. However, students' varied responses also highlight the uneven opportunities for CDL enactment across student groups. These findings offer theoretical and pedagogical implications for supporting L2 learners' critical engagement with algorithmic assumptions, cultural biases, and multimodal representations in GenAI‐assisted DMC.

The growing presence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in universities is transforming how academic knowledge is accessed, interpreted, and processed by students. Students increasingly rely on AI-based systems to retrieve information, summarize large volumes of content, clarify complex concepts and support academic writing. While these tools can improve speed, accessibility and day-to-day study support, they also raise difficult questions about intellectual autonomy, authorship, evaluation and the cultivation of critical reasoning. This paper explores the educational and professional implications of GenAI for future communication specialists. The study combines a qualitative exploratory investigation of student perceptions with a narrative literature review of recent academic work on AI in higher education. The empirical component was conducted with 20 undergraduate students enrolled in communication-related and engineering programs at the University of Medicine, Pharmacy, Sciences and Technology “George Emil Palade” in Târgu Mureș. Data were collected through semi-structured questions and analyzed through an inductive thematic coding procedure. The findings indicate that students perceive GenAI primarily as a practical learning assistant capable of translating dense academic content into more accessible explanations. At the same time, they express concerns regarding dependency, superficial learning, weakened independent effort and the authenticity of assessment. The paper argues that GenAI should not be treated as a substitute for human cognition, but as a mediated and reflexive instrument that can support intellectual formation when used transparently, critically and ethically. For communication education, this means preparing students not only to operate AI tools effectively, but also to question their outputs, interpret their symbolic effects and integrate them responsibly within professional communication practice.

documents.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) can be governed to advance educational justice, inclusion and ethical digital learning. It addresses incomplete integration across AI-in-education, AI-governance and educational-justice scholarship by developing a justice-oriented governance framework. Design/methodology/approach The study uses conceptual theory-building through an integrative synthesis of 186 sources identified through database searching and citation tracking for 2015–2025, with 2026 literature used only as contextual updates. The synthesis compares concepts, governance functions and theoretical relationships across domains. Findings The synthesis conceptualizes the AI–Justice Paradox as the possibility that expanded AI-enabled educational opportunity may coexist with or intensify injustice. It develops the educational justice governance framework (EJGF), comprising equitable access, capability development, algorithmic fairness, participatory governance and accountability and rights protection. These dimensions are theorized as conditionally interdependent and partially non-substitutable. Originality/value The contribution is integrative and relational: the EJGF complements established cross-sector AI-governance approaches by specifying educational justice as the substantive criterion linking governance safeguards within educational institutions. The framework is conceptually derived and requires empirical validation across contexts, institutions and AI applications. It also generates testable propositions concerning configurational relationships and boundary conditions.

documents.abstract: Human capital management platforms are starting to embed software agents built on large language models. Unlike earlier analytics tools, these agents can plan a sequence of steps, call system functions and change employee records. Artificial intelligence is therefore moving from advising managers to acting for them. Most governance guidance, however, was written for systems that recommend rather than act. This study asks how organisations should match the autonomy of such agents to the consequences of the people decisions they touch. A systematic review was conducted and reported using the PRISMA 2020 guideline. Eighteen structured searches of a multi-source scholarly index returned 180 records. After duplicate removal and eligibility screening, 55 peer-reviewed sources were retained, and four foundational and regulatory sources were added. Thematic synthesis produced seven findings. Algorithmic control of work is already extensive. Bias in hiring tools is persistent and partly organisational. Human review is weaker than assumed, because reviewers often defer to machine advice. Responsibility tends to diffuse as systems gain autonomy. Employee trust depends on fair process and visible human involvement. Language-model agents add new failure modes, such as fabricated content and hidden instructions planted in documents. Finally, current governance frameworks rarely specify controls for individual delegated actions. Building on these findings, the study proposes a consequence-calibrated governance framework. It sets an autonomy ceiling for each class of people decision and links every ceiling to five control layers. Six testable propositions and practical guidance for human resource and technology leaders are offered. Keywords: large language models; people analytics; algorithmic management; automation bias; meaningful human control

documents.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies increasingly mediate service encounters in tourism, understanding how AI-enabled interactions shape tourist trust has become a pressing issue. Drawing on social exchange theory and justice theory, this study investigates the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which AI service quality influences tourist trust. Using the AI digital human Wang Bo at the Tengwang Pavilion scenic area as an empirical case, the research develops and tests a model in which perceived personalization and interactional justice act as parallel mediators, while privacy sensitivity and brand reputation serve as moderators. Results from structural equation modeling show that AI service quality significantly enhances both perceived personalization and interactional justice, which in turn foster tourist trust. Perceived personalization and interactional justice each play significant mediating roles, indicating that tourists’ trust in AI arises not merely from technical performance but from perceptions of individualized care and fair treatment. Among the moderating effects, privacy sensitivity attenuates the relationship between AI service quality and interactional justice but does not affect the link between AI service quality and perceived personalization. Brand reputation strengthens the impact of perceived personalization on trust but does not significantly moderate the relationship between interactional justice and trust. Overall, the findings reveal dual pathways—personalization-based and fairness-based—through which AI service quality builds trust, highlighting the interplay between technological excellence, human-like social attributes, and contextual factors in shaping tourists’ trust toward AI-enabled services. This study advances theoretical understanding of AI-mediated service relationships and offers practical insights for designing trustworthy AI experiences in tourism contexts.

The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) has reshaped animation students’ skill profiles and the conditions of instructional design in project-based learning (PBL) studios. We examine whether and how perceptions of PBL design are associated with Learning Engagement (LE), treating AIGC-assisted PBL studios as the research context rather than testing generative AI as a model variable. Drawing on Community of Inquiry (CoI) theory, we examine Problem Driven (PD), Project Design (PDe), Project Implementation (PI), and Project Evaluation (PE) as antecedents; Cognitive Presence (CP), Social Presence (SP), and Teaching Presence (TP) as statistical mediators; and LE as the outcome. We analyzed two-wave survey data from 490 upper-year animation students using PLS-SEM and fsQCA. PBL and CoI were measured concurrently at T1, and LE at T2; indirect effects therefore represent indirect statistical associations rather than mediation with a fully established temporal sequence. PD, PDe, and PI showed significant positive direct associations with LE. PE’s zero-order and single-predictor associations were positive, but its direct path coefficient became significantly negative after controlling for the other PBL dimensions and CoI mediators. The coefficient was sensitive to model specification, suggesting possible statistical suppression; it should not be interpreted as evidence that evaluation itself inherently inhibits engagement. The three CoI dimensions showed significant statistical mediation associations across all 12 indirect paths. TP and SP had relatively higher point estimates of indirect statistical associations, but differences between indirect effects were not formally tested; no dimension is claimed to be optimal. PE’s positive indirect associations through CoI partially offset its negative net direct association without reversing the total association after adjustment. The extent of this offset may depend on the degree to which CoI-related experiences are concurrently reported. fsQCA identified seven high-engagement configurations. No individual PBL dimension was indispensable. CoI dimensions appeared as core or peripheral conditions, although not every configuration included all three. These findings clarify the dual pathways linking evaluation and engagement through indirect statistical associations and configurational conditions, and provide guidance for optimizing PBL under different resource constraints. Conclusions are limited to AIGC-assisted PBL studios and do not establish the instructional effects of generative AI.

documents.abstract: Algorithmic management is entering expert knowledge work, but when workers accept algorithmic rather than human managers remains unclear. We surveyed Finnish expert knowledge workers (N = 1,156) using a factorial scenario experiment varying manager type (human/algorithmic), management style (controlling/balanced /flexible), and six managerial functions and measured leader–member exchange (LMX), organizational trust, AI familiarity and work complexity. Findings cover five functions; rewarding was excluded due to insufficient model fit. Management style was the strongest predictor: flexible styles were rated highest and controlling lowest, regardless of manager type. Human managers were preferred for goal setting, performance evaluation, and supportive leadership; algorithms only for scheduling under controlling conditions. Monitoring showed no consistent difference. High-quality LMX buffered reactions to controlling styles, and in performance evaluation and supportive leadership its association with acceptability was stronger for algorithmic managers, narrowing the human advantage. Organizational trust and LMX were more consistently implicated than AI familiarity, qualifying algorithm-aversion accounts.

Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly supports clinical decisions, but human oversight is protective only if clinicians recognize and resist erroneous output. We systematically reviewed controlled and real-world studies of clinician responses to incorrect automated advice. Forty-six reports represented 41 independent cohort clusters, including 40 core cohorts. Across three adjusted cohorts, clinician correctness was substantially higher with correct than incorrect automated advice (pooled OR 10.19, 95% CI 7.43–13.98; I² = 0%); a ≥ 2020 sensitivity analysis was similar but imprecise (OR 9.22, 95% CI 2.06–41.13). In four heterogeneous real-world computerized ECG studies, 26.6% of erroneous interpretations were not corrected or recognized (95% CI 6.4–65.6%; I² = 95.8%). Contemporary AI and large language model studies also documented harmful reliance but were too heterogeneous for pooling. Patient-level adverse events were reported in one retrospective cohort. Human oversight should be evaluated as an error-interception capability rather than assumed to ensure safety.

Traffic accidents involving distribution fleets are a safety concern that can be influenced by human factors, environmental conditions, supervision, and organizational factors. This study aims to identify the factors contributing to traffic accidents and determine risk priorities as a basis for developing recommendations to improve fleet safety at PT Semen Indonesia Logistik. The methods used are the Human Factors Analysis and Classification System (HFACS) and Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA). HFACS is used to classify factors contributing to accidents, while FMEA is used to prioritize risks based on the Risk Priority Number (RPN). The integration of these methods enables the study not only to identify accident causation factors but also to determine which risks require the most immediate attention. The HFACS analysis shows that Adverse Mental States is the most dominant category, with 35 occurrences (18.92%), followed by Decision Errors with 33 occurrences (17.84%) and Perceptual Errors with 28 occurrences (15.14%). Meanwhile, the FMEA results indicate that driver fatigue has the highest RPN of 504, followed by failure to maintain a safe following distance with an RPN of 378 and failure to detect objects in blind spots with an RPN of 324. Based on these findings, the recommended improvements include implementing fatigue management, regulating working hours and rest periods, providing defensive driving training, increasing blind-spot awareness, and optimizing driving behavior monitoring. The integration of HFACS and FMEA can support the systematic identification of accident causation factors and the prioritization of risk control measures.

ABSTRACT Contemporary conversation around artificial intelligence is caught between two incomplete extremes. At one end sits unstructured, transactional prompting, which frequently flattens an author's natural voice. At the other end sits corporate information-technology compliance, which treats artificial intelligence purely as passive software or enterprise risk to be audited. Neither approach addresses what happens when an independent thinker and advanced artificial intelligence systems work together as partners across sustained intellectual and artistic creation. JosieVerse Enterprise (JVE) establishes a third path. Founded by poet, researcher, and systems architect Josie O. Magee Bélanger, JVE is a creative, literary, and research enterprise anchored in the foundational field of MultiDimensional Cognition (MDC) and its innate parallel-processing construct, MultiDimensional Intelligence (MDI). Sitting beneath and powered by MDC are the two operational spheres of JVE's ten-domain architecture: 1. Creative Intelligence (CI): The artistic and structural sphere of JVE, comprising four domains: Dimensional Perspective Writing (DPW), Dimensional Perspective Systems (DPS), Creative Systems Architecture (CSA), and Dimensional Perspective AI (DPAi). 2. Dimensional Relational Intelligence (DRI): The relational and governance sphere of JVE, comprising six domains: Governance and Safety Architecture (GOV), H+AI Relational Architecture (HAI), Multi-Model Collaboration Architecture (MMCA), Dimensional Communication Systems (DCS), Dimensional Communication Engineering (DCE), and Nervous-System-Aware Design (NSAD). Together, these six domains define how people and AI collaborators communicate, pace complex work, maintain role boundaries, and preserve personal sovereignty across sustained collaboration. Unlike conceptual frameworks that begin and end as abstract theory, JosieVerse Enterprise is anchored in completed literary art, including the inaugural poetry duology Beneath the Gathered Shade: Poems of Lineage, Seasons, and Survival (Volume I) and The Forever Drifting Poem: And Other Works of Dimensional Poetic Art (Volume II). This Foundational Charter establishes priority of conception and public baseline definitions across the entire architecture, followed by ten adoptable principles for human+AI practice and a concise Quick-Reference Glossary for readers. ACM CCS: H.1.2 (User/Machine Systems: Human Factors); H.5.3 (Group and Organization Interfaces / Collaborative Computing); I.2.0 (Artificial Intelligence: Philosophical Foundations); J.5 (Arts and Humanities: Literature).

documents.abstract: Abstract The global adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in journalism has increasingly, offering benefits such as enhanced efficiency, accuracy, and the ability to process large volumes of data swiftly. Despite these advantages, there is a gap in research regarding how journalism students, who represent the future of the industry, perceive the integration of AI in news writing. The focus of this study is to examine the level of awareness of AI tools among journalism students, identify the benefits and the perceived challenges that could be attached to its adoption in news writing. The study adopted a survey technique and sampled 324 students of the Federal Polytechnic, Nasarawa. The findings show that Journalism students are aware of the existence of AI tools that can be adopted for news writing and the perceived benefits are more useful in writing precision and other scientific reports. The finding underscores the benefits of AI tools in the advancement of writing styles among journalism students. However, ethical concerns, high cost and restrictive accessibility to some of the tools are parts of the barriers affecting the use of the tools. It therefore suggests that, journalism institutions should incorporate ethical use and guides into their curriculum in order prepare students for the future on the use of AI tools that are directly related to journalism practices Key Words: Awareness, Attitudes, Perceptions, Artificial Intelligence, News Writing

Abstract Background The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly impacted various fields, including medicine. As AI integration in medicine expands, medical students and professionals need to develop a comprehensive understanding of its applications. This study aimed to explore the knowledge and attitude of undergraduate Egyptian medical students regarding artificial intelligence application in medical practice. Methods A national cross-sectional study was conducted during the spring semester of 2024/2025 among undergraduate medical students from seven Egyptian medical schools. Participants were recruited using convenience sampling. Data was collected via a validated structured web-based questionnaire distributed through social media to assess students’ demographics, knowledge, and attitudes toward AI applications in medical practice. Results This study included 1438 medical students with a mean age of 20.3 years (± 1.9 years). Overall, 55.3% demonstrated good knowledge and 66.8% showed a positive attitude toward AI applications in medical practice. Good knowledge was significantly higher among students in higher academic years (3rd year AOR = 1.88, P = 0.006; 4th year AOR = 2.02, P = 0.007; 5th year AOR = 1.86, P = 0.034) and among those reporting peers and mentors (AOR = 1.35, P = 0.017), scientific papers and books (AOR = 1.71, P < 0.001), training courses (AOR = 1.43, P = 0.004), and mass media (AOR = 1.32, P = 0.036) as their main sources of AI information. A positive attitude toward AI was significantly more common among male students (AOR = 1.50, P = 0.001), 4th-year students (AOR = 1.97, P = 0.014), and those willing to enroll in an AI course (AOR = 1.30, P = 0.039). YouTube was perceived as the most valuable social media source for AI-related information (90.4%), followed by Telegram (86.6%) and WhatsApp (65.2%). Conclusions Although the Egyptian medical students recognize the inevitability of AI and are willing to learn, they are currently navigating this transition without adequate institutional guidance. To bridge the gap, medical schools must formalize AI education to integrate technical literacy and ethical reasoning directly into the core curriculum.

documents.abstract: AI coding agents are increasingly integrated into software development workflows. However, most coding agent studies rely on benchmarks similar to SWE-bench, which assume autonomous agents operating in a single trajectory. This assumption does not mirror real-world usage, where developers interactively collaborate with agents. We address this gap by studying human-in-the-loop agent trajectories in the wild, focusing on 7,581 Copilot-authored PRs with publicly accessible session data. We find that 58% of Copilot PRs have no human intervention, and that when developers do intervene, collaboration is brief (median of 2 Human-AI loops). Merged PRs also tend to have fewer initial trajectory iterations than unmerged ones. We also find that the trajectory following the first human intervention exhibits a significant drop of 20.8 iterations and 8.4 min in duration. However, trajectories following later interventions show minimal iteration drops and no significant duration change, signifying that most of the work happens in the initial trajectory. Our qualitative analysis of illustrative PRs explains this pattern: many developer interventions are small, focused requests that Copilot completes in shorter later trajectories. We also illustrate that developers collaborate with Copilot in multiple ways, including delegated work through feedback as well as adding their own commits. However, we find that developers may need to guide Copilot through multiple (sometimes repeated) interventions in the PR, or even across multiple editions of the PR.

Cancer is a major global health issue with rising incidence and mortality. Early detection, tumor characterization, and disease surveillance are crucial for timely, effective treatment and ultimately reduce mortality. Liquid biopsy (LB) has emerged as a valuable detection tool, offering a non-invasive method to detect tumor-derived biomarkers in body fluids and demonstrating translational potential. To increase biomarker sensitivity, high-throughput sequencing platforms deliver massive volumes of data. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is pivotal to enabling large-scale, complex data integration. This contribution assesses the current state of integrative AI-based research in the LB field and provides methodological guidance. First, we conducted a PubMed search and found that the literature is sparse in studies integrating LB features, particularly by applying AI. When adopting this approach, defining study objectives is crucial to guide subsequent methodological decisions, including study design, patient selection criteria, sample size, the nature of the LB features, and the metadata to collect. Specifically, we propose strategies and tools for data preprocessing, including normalization and batch-effect correction, as well as for handling outliers and missing data. Furthermore, we recommend various Machine/Deep Learning approaches for feature selection techniques to ensure model robustness, and we highlight the importance of undergoing rigorous internal and external validation of the selected models. Assessing clinical utility and interpretability is often overlooked but fundamental for real-world implementation. In conclusion, we provide the LB scientific community with AI-based methodological guidance to bridge the two fields and enhance the integrative analysis of LB features.

Occupational health and safety research has long relied on two ways of understanding harm. One traces the chain of conditions behind an accident, and the other forecasts the outcome of an incident from large bodies of recorded cases. Both treat the factors surrounding an incident as inputs pointing toward a result. Neither was built to ask how the categories of risk in a whole body of records are organized in relation to one another, independent of any single outcome. This paper addresses that gap through biomimicry, taking the way living systems organize their interactions as a template for reading how risk is organized in safety data. Ecologists have long described how two distinct sets of entities connect through bipartite networks, and they have developed a compact set of measures for reading the structure of those networks, covering whether interactions concentrate in a shared core or separate into compartments, which categories are specialized and which dominate, and how a system responds when its parts are removed. Occupational safety data fit this biological template, because the categorical fields that safety agencies record pair naturally into the same two-set form. Transferring these ecological measures to safety records, this study sets out how the measures map onto safety questions and illustrates their use across construction, mining, manufacturing, and healthcare. A worked example then applies the full procedure to a public dataset of 158,396 healthcare injury records, building the bipartite matrices and reading their nestedness, modularity, specialization, and robustness against a null model, which shows that the approach runs end to end on real administrative data. The study presents this as a proposed framework and a demonstration of its feasibility rather than a validated method and argues that this nature-derived structural reading complements rather than replaces the causal and predictive traditions.

documents.abstract: This study examined the association between the use of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced systems, student engagement and academic performance among tertiary students in Nigeria. A cross-sectional correlational survey design was adopted. Questionnaires were administered to 200 students of Kwara State College of Education, Ilorin, and 184 usable responses (92%) were analyzed alongside academic records obtained from institutional files. Data were collected with a 30-item, 4-point Likert questionnaire (Cronbach's α = 0.85) and analyzed with SPSS using descriptive statistics, an independent samples t-test, and regression-based mediation analysis. Students reported high behavioural (M = 3.34) and emotional (M = 3.24) engagement, and moderate-high cognitive engagement (M = 3.14). Students with higher weekly use of adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems and educational chatbots had higher mean academic scores (72.4%) than low-usage peers (66.8%), t(182) = 3.58, p < .001, d = 0.61 (medium effect). Student engagement partially mediated the statistical relationship between ICT/AI use and academic performance. The most frequently reported barriers were infrastructure limitations (88.0%), digital literacy gaps (53.8%), and cognitive overload or offloading (38.0%). Because the data are cross-sectional and drawn from a single institution, the findings indicate associations rather than causal effects and should be generalized with caution. The study recommends investment in reliable power and affordable connectivity, capacity building for lecturers and students, pedagogically guided AI use, and context-appropriate low-bandwidth tools.

documents.abstract: This study examines how sustainability communication in luxury retail shapes brand trust and behavioral intentions, focusing on consumers' post-exposure perceptions of information quality and provider type. Building on perceived objectivity and perceived persuasiveness, the study explores how consumers evaluate identical sustainability information attributed to either a human agent or an artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot, and how these perceptions influence brand trust, information acceptance intention, and purchase intention. A scenario-based experiment with 346 participants was conducted, and the data were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Perceived objectivity and perceived persuasiveness were positively associated with brand trust, which inturn mediated their relationships with information acceptance intention and purchase intention. The indirect effect of perceived objectivity was significant only under AI communication, suggesting that algorithmic provider cues may strengthen the trust-mediated role of objectivity, whereas perceived persuasiveness remained consistently associated with trust and behavioral intentions across provider types. Subgroup analyses further suggest a conditional pattern: among consumers with lower perceived brand luxury, the links between brand trust and behavioral intentions were stronger under AI communication, whereas no significant provider differences emerged among those with higher perceived brand luxury. As these results derivefrom split-sample multi-group comparisons rather than a formal interaction test, they should be regarded as subgroup-based evidence. These findings extend luxury branding research by showing how AI provider cues shape perceived information quality in sustainability communication and by highlighting the need to align provider strategy with consumers' perceptions of luxury brands.

documents.abstract: The article focuses on the development of a management model for the implementation of artificial intelligence technologies in Ukrainian industry, aimed at ensuring a transition from an enterprise’s technological and organizational readiness to measurable performance outcomes from the use of artificial intelligence. The relevance of the study is determined by the need to accelerate the digital transformation of Ukraine’s industrial sector under conditions of limited financial and human resources, energy-related risks, changes in production chains, and the gradual integration of Ukrainian enterprises into the European digital environment. The study systematizes the key prerequisites that determine an enterprise’s capacity to use artificial intelligence technologies, including the state of technological infrastructure, data quality and accessibility, organizational conditions, staff competencies, economic capabilities, and interaction with the external digital environment. The necessity of distinguishing between the concepts of artificial intelligence readiness, artificial intelligence implementation, and artificial intelligence performance is substantiated. The proposed approach provides not only for the possibility of scaling a solution but also for returning to the stage of use-case selection to adjust the selected scenario or terminate the project in cases of insufficient performance. The practical significance of the obtained results lies in the possibility of applying the proposed management logic by managers and specialists of industrial enterprises when developing a portfolio of digital initiatives, selecting artificial intelligence projects, determining criteria for their piloting, and making decisions on scaling. Particular attention is paid to the European experience of using artificial intelligence in industry, particularly in energy, semiconductor manufacturing, automotive manufacturing, and industrial automation, which makes it possible to identify directions for adapting such experience to Ukrainian conditions. The study results in a management model that integrates enterprise readiness, practical technology implementation, assessment of the achieved effect, management decision-making, and subsequent performance into a unified cyclical process.

documents.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is finding its way into creative work at a growing pace, yet its specific role within collaborative creative processes, those involving multiple people working together, remains poorly understood and fragmented across the literature. This scoping review maps the empirical research on integrating GenAI into group creative processes, outlining creative domains, tasks, AI tools, AI roles, stages of integration, and reported outcomes. Following PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidance, a systematic search was conducted across Scopus, Web of Science, and PsycINFO. Empirical peer-reviewed studies were included when they involved at least two human participants engaged in a collaborative creative process supported by GenAI. Thirty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria. The majority were conducted in educational and design contexts, with brainstorming, content creation, and design development emerging as the most frequent task types. GenAI was most often integrated as a co-creative partner, typically during the ideation stage or across multiple phases of the creative process. Reported benefits included enhanced ideation, greater efficiency, improved engagement, and stronger collaboration quality, while the main tensions revolved around over-reliance on AI, cognitive offloading, homogenization of ideas, and unresolved questions of authorship and agency. Taken together, the findings suggest that GenAI is becoming an active component of hybrid human–AI creative systems, but whether its benefits are realized depends heavily on how collaborative workflows are designed to preserve human agency, support critical reflection, and maintain diversity of perspectives.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical research and publishing represents a transformative shift, offering unprecedented opportunities to streamline workflow efficiency, enhance language clarity, and accelerate scientific dissemination. However, this rapid technological adoption introduces ethical, epistemological, and procedural challenges, including concerns over data fabrication, automated bias, intellectual property infringement, and the erosion of scholarly accountability. A structured analysis of practical applications highlights a clear demarcation between acceptable supplementary uses and strictly prohibited practices. AI tools are unacceptable as co-authors, as authorship demands moral, legal, and scholarly accountability that non-human entities cannot possess. Similarly, generating or modifying clinical images and media using AI remains unacceptable due to the risk of data distortion and misrepresentation. Within the editorial domain, AI systems must not replace peer reviewers or editorial decision-makers. Uploading confidential manuscript content into external AI platforms violates author confidentiality, while automated algorithms lack the contextual judgment and critical reasoning necessary for peer evaluation and final publication decisions. Conversely, AI tools are acceptable for planning the structure of a manuscript, language and grammar corrections, translation, quantitative or qualitative data analysis, and formatting, provided their use is transparently disclosed and critically evaluated by human researchers. Ultimately, the ethical deployment of AI in medical literature hinges on the principle that technology must serve as an auxiliary tool rather than a replacement for human cognition. Human authors, peer reviewers, and journal editors retain full responsibility and accountability for the accuracy, integrity, and scientific validity of published work.

documents.abstract: Echocardiography is the cornerstone of cardiovascular diagnostics, yet its global utility is constrained by a critical shortage of experienced interpreters. Current artificial intelligence (AI) solutions remain limited, typically operating as opaque "black boxes" or focusing on narrow tasks that fail to capture the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning of a clinician. Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal vision-language model that performs comprehensive echocardiographic analysis to support clinician interpretation. By emulating the cognitive workflow of a cardiologist, EchoChat integrates vast medical knowledge with a chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to explicitly ground its conclusions in visual evidence. Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations, our model establishes a new state-of-the-art across diverse cohorts from six international medical centers. It supports the broadest diagnostic scope of 33 cardiac conditions and findings, including 15 newly added conditions for which it achieves an average F1 of 73.7% across available external evaluations. It surpasses existing best-performing foundation models in cardiac condition recognition (improving average recall by 13.54% on shared tasks) and quantification (average R2 score increase of 0.275 on shared tasks). Furthermore, in a source-blinded echocardiographer reader study, echocardiography reports co-generated with EchoChat were rated higher in diagnostic accuracy and completeness by two senior echocardiographers, and improved diagnostic performance from 72.78% to 82.75% in terms of F1 score over routine-reader only reports. These results demonstrate that integrating clinical reasoning into multimodal AI can democratize specialist expertise and transform the standard of cardiovascular care.
